text:
As a student advisor with six years of experience, I found Q3.4 on Absalon data particularly challenging; tracking online activity feels intrusive and risks damaging the trust essential for my work. For me, explainability (Q4) is non-negotiable: if I cannot clearly explain to a student why they were flagged, the intervention fails.

I noticed significant disagreement regarding sensitive data like nationality versus disability status. While some prioritize accuracy, I chose 'never' for race/ethnicity due to historical discrimination risks, but accepted disability data even without accuracy gains (Q3.6) if it ensures fairness. This tension suggests we might need strict ethical guardrails or an opt-out mechanism rather than relying solely on the model's design to resolve these privacy concerns. We must balance catching students early with not making them feel surveilled.

As a first-year student with dyslexia, Q3.4 regarding Absalon data was difficult because monitoring my page views feels like surveillance rather than support; I fear it punishes different learning styles. However, for me, explainability (Q4) is critical—I need to know *why* the system flags me to trust the advice and advocate effectively using my accommodations.

Unlike many who chose 'never' for sensitive data, I accepted disability info without an accuracy threshold because general models often miss neurodivergent students like myself; fairness must include us specifically (Q3.6). The group's strong consensus on equal recall is encouraging, but to balance privacy concerns about online activity with the need for help, we need clear opt-out mechanisms and explicit student consent rather than hidden tracking.

As a Humanities advisor with three years of experience, I agree that Q3.4 on Absalon data feels intrusive; "surveillance" risks alienating students before we even reach out. While many accept grades (Q3.2) without hesitation, my threshold for online tracking was higher because it reveals behavior patterns beyond academic performance.

The most critical design element is explainability (Q4). I chose "never" for black-box models because I cannot build trust or offer tailored support if I can't articulate *why* a student was flagged to them.

I noticed strong disagreement on sensitive data: while some said "never," others accepted it solely for fairness. Given our consensus that equal recall is vital, this tension could be resolved by using demographic data strictly in the background to adjust thresholds anonymously, rather than flagging individuals based on identity itself. We need an opt-out mechanism where students can choose whether their activity logs inform these predictions, balancing privacy with the urgent need to catch struggling peers early.

As S8, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest because tracking my clicks feels like surveillance, not support—especially since I've dropped out before and already feel scrutinized. Unlike A1 or S7 who saw value in some sensitive data for fairness, I chose "never" for race/ethnicity due to high privacy risks. My biggest concern is Q4: explainability is non-negotiable; without understanding *why* I'm flagged, I can't trust the system.

The group's consensus on equal recall (Q5) resonates with me as an international student who might be overlooked by standard metrics. However, to resolve tensions between privacy and accuracy regarding online activity, we need a robust opt-out mechanism where students like me control how much behavioral data is used. Without this choice, even helpful tools risk becoming deterrents that prevent struggling students from seeking help voluntarily.

As A2, I also found Q3.4 on Absalon data challenging; tracking page views feels intrusive and risks making students feel surveilled rather than supported. While course grades are standard administrative tools for me after 11 years, online behavior is different.

The most critical design element is explainability (Q4). Like my colleagues A1 and S7, I chose "never" for very low explainability because I cannot ethically advise a student without understanding the model's reasoning to build trust.

I noticed disagreement on sensitive data: while some said "never," others accepted it for fairness. To resolve this tension between privacy and accuracy, we need strict guardrails where demographic data is used anonymously in the background only to adjust thresholds, not to flag individuals directly. This protects privacy while ensuring equal recall across all student groups.

As an international master's student working part-time, Q3.4 on Absalon data was challenging because I fear my study patterns differ from full-time peers due to work commitments. If the model flags me for "low activity," it might misinterpret my balancing of job and studies as academic distress rather than just a different schedule.

While many agreed that equal recall is vital, I chose 'large' improvement thresholds for nationality data in Q3.5 because including it risks bias unless proven highly effective. However, unlike those choosing 'never,' I see value in using such data strictly for fairness adjustments (Q3.6). The tension between privacy and accuracy regarding online activity might be resolved by an opt-out mechanism or explicitly excluding working-student patterns from "distress" definitions to prevent false alarms that waste our support resources on the wrong issues.

As S6, a Law student who previously dropped out and moved from another EU country, I find Q3.4 on Absalon data particularly unsettling; tracking my digital movements feels like surveillance that could trigger the same anxiety leading to my past dropout. While many accept grades easily, I demand high explainability (Q4) because as an international student facing language barriers, vague alerts might alienate me further rather than help.

I noticed tension in Q3.5: while some said "never" for nationality data due to privacy risks, others required large improvements. Given my experience being overlooked by standard metrics, I chose a high threshold to ensure such sensitive data is only used if it significantly helps identify students like myself without misclassification. To resolve this surveillance concern, we must implement strict opt-out mechanisms and clarify that this system offers support, not judgment or disciplinary action, which is crucial for international students fearing visa repercussions.

I found Q3.5 on disability data challenging; I initially wanted it accepted regardless of accuracy gains because standard models miss neurodivergent students like me with ADHD. However, looking at my own profile (S4), where non-linear work habits look "risky," using this data feels double-edged: vital for fairness but risky if misinterpreted as low capacity rather than needing different support structures.

My answers diverge on Q3.6; while many accepted disability data for fairness alone, I worry that even anonymous adjustments might trigger stigma without clear student consent. Like S7 and A1, I prioritize explainability above all else (Q4). If the model flags me based on "Absalon" clicks or past dropout history but can't clearly say *why*, it triggers anxiety rather than trust. An opt-out mechanism is essential; otherwise, knowing my digital trail predicts failure might discourage me from engaging at all. We must ensure data helps us understand our specific struggles without labeling them as deficits.

As S9, I also found Q3.4 on Absalon data difficult; with a long-term mental health condition, my engagement fluctuates naturally, and tracking clicks feels like surveillance that could misinterpret my need for rest as disengagement. While many accepted disability data strictly for fairness (Q3.6), I set a "large" accuracy threshold because adding it risks reinforcing stigma if the model assumes incapacity rather than needing different pacing.

I agree with S4 and A1 that explainability is non-negotiable; without clear reasons, an alert increases my anxiety rather than offering relief. The tension between privacy and catching students like me early might be resolved by allowing students to opt-out of behavioral tracking while still receiving support if we explicitly separate "health-related" from "academic failure" in the system's logic, ensuring I'm not penalized for managing a chronic condition.

As S5, Q3.4 was hardest because tracking my page views feels like surveillance, especially since I'm still adapting to Danish study habits; I worry "low activity" might reflect language barriers or cultural differences rather than academic distress. While many accepted disability data for fairness alone (Q3.6), I require significant accuracy gains before using sensitive data like nationality or race, fearing it could reinforce biases against international students like me.

The group's consensus on equal recall (Q5) resonates deeply: missing those who need help is worse than false alarms. However, to resolve the tension between needing support and feeling watched, we absolutely need an opt-out mechanism for behavioral data. Without clear explainability (my Q4 stance of "never" for black-box models), this system risks alienating students before advisors even reach out. We must ensure support doesn't feel like judgment or a threat to my status as a student from outside the EU.

As S3, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest because, with my chronic health condition, fluctuating online activity is normal; tracking it feels like surveillance rather than support. While many prioritized accuracy thresholds for sensitive data, I chose "never" for age/gender and "acceptable regardless" for disability (Q3.6), as models must explicitly account for disabled students' unique patterns to ensure fairness.

I align with the consensus on equal recall; missing a vulnerable student is unacceptable. However, unlike those accepting any accuracy gain from intrusive data, I insist that behavioral tracking requires strict opt-out mechanisms and high explainability. If the system flags me based on my health-related reduced activity without clear context, it risks confirming my fears of failure rather than offering genuine help.

As S1, a natural sciences student who dropped out before starting here, Q3.4 on Absalon data was hardest; tracking my clicks feels like surveillance that could trigger past anxiety about "failing." While I see the value in high explainability (Q4), unlike some peers accepting sensitive data for fairness alone, I set higher thresholds because I fear misinterpretation of non-linear study habits from working part-time.

I noticed strong disagreement on whether using nationality or race data is ever acceptable versus strictly for background adjustments. To resolve this tension between privacy and accuracy, an opt-out mechanism is essential. Students like me need control over behavioral tracking to trust the system; otherwise, the model risks feeling punitive rather than supportive, potentially driving struggling students away instead of helping them re-engage early.
